entry.title: Streamlining Event Updates: Integrating Google Calendar with Google Spaces

link.title: Streamlining Event Updates: Integrating Google Calendar with Google Spaces

entry.content:
In my current office, we heavily use Google Calendar. The norm is such that when someone is out, away, or, there is an important event we set that with duration as an event in the Office Calendar. To spice things up — we used to have a Bot that would check up after a while if there was an event that had been added to the Calendar since the last time it checked. If it finds something like that the Bot would take the information from that event and send a notification (as a message) in our office’s common Google Space, named as — Events.

Interestingly, a couple of days back my CTO’s subscription ran out of the trial period. And, this is where I come to muscle myself up to replace that task with something I never have worked on!

So, in this guide, we’ll walk through setting up an integration between Google Calendar and a designated Google Space using Google Apps Script

Yes, you heard it right! Google has a service that anyone can use for running JavaScript Code when you wish, or as a Cronjob. The primary purpose of it is to provide communication across Google Services, say — you provide a value in a specific Google Sheet and it will change something in another Google Doc.

Anyway, Let’s dive in!

Part 1 | Setting Up Your Google Space

  • Access your Google Space, like “Events”. 🎉
  • Navigate to Space Settings > Apps & Integrations > Web Hooks.
  • Create a WebHook, name it, and even add a funky avatar! 🌈
  • Save the settings and grab the generated Webhook URL.

Check out below, how it will look when EventBuzz sends the Notification Message in the Google Space -

Part 2 | Configuring Google Apps Script

  • Start by creating a new project on script.google.com, how about naming it “EventBuzz”? 📝
  • Open the Code.gs file, and let’s sprinkle in some magic by copying the code in Code.gs from our GitHub repository into this file. 🧙‍♂️✨ It will look like this -

Part 3 | Integrating Your Calendar

  • Go into the Google Calendar in which you are interested to check in for new events, for my case I am using — Office Calendar.
  • Go to Settings > Integrate Calendar and find the Calendar ID, it’s your secret key! 🗝️

Here’s where you will look for Calendar ID -

It will look like this -

Part 4 | Defining Script Properties

  • Within your Google Apps Script project (our case — EventBuzz), head to Project Settings > Script Properties. It’s like adding your special ingredients!

On a serious note, it’s for security reasons. In this way, we don’t put any of our secret sauce in the code. The code becomes independent of the Secrets/Credentials it needs to work on because we are injecting it from outside. Also, if these secrets/credentials need to be changed, we can do it centrally, we don’t need to change our code.

  • Add two Properties — ‘companyChannelWebhookUrl’ (paste your Webhook URL in the value field that you added in the Events - Google Space) and ‘officeCalendarId’ (paste your Calendar ID in the value field). 🌟 And, Save. It will look something like this -

Part 5 | Establishing Triggers

  • Get trigger-happy in the Triggers section of your Google Apps Script project.
  • Set up a trigger for ‘sendNewEventsToChat’ for every 15 minutes, ensuring everyone’s in the loop! 🎊 This will be the setting for this trigger -
  • Additionally, create another trigger for ‘clearStoredEventIds’ to tidy up every 5 minutes, maintaining a clean event log. 🧹 The Settings for this trigger will be like this -

Voila! 🎩✨

You’ve just unleashed an automated wizard that updates your Google Space with new events from your chosen Google Calendar. This magic trick ensures seamless collaboration and timely communication within your team or community. Keep the magic alive! 🌟✨

entry.title: Unleashing the Power of Bash: A Comparision with Python for Data Processing

link.title: Unleashing the Power of Bash: A Comparision with Python for Data Processing

entry.content:
Excerpt:

Recently, while working with a large text dataset, I found myself diving deep into the world of bash scripting to unlock the potential for mining patterns, extracting information, and parsing data.

As a Pythonista, I predominantly rely on Python for scripting and enterprise-level development. However, this experience with bash made me realize the true power that developers can harness by incorporating bash into their development pipelines.

What is the Problem I am solving?

First, let’s look at a folder structure to understand the Problem.

In my specific task, I needed to do the following -

  • Traverse directories within parent folders.
  • Find XML files within the directories.
  • For each XML file:
    → Locate a specific node containing a PDF embedded in Base64 format.
    → Extract the Base64 data.
    → Export the PDF.
    → Split the PDF into individual images representing each page.
    → Perform OCR using Tesseract on each image to extract text.
    → Merge the text splits into a single file representing the PDF.

Fire in the Hole — BASH!

I decided to tackle this task using bash, leveraging its capabilities to run the subroutine on the entire Dataset. The execution time for the task was approximately 132 minutes. Curiosity sparked within me, and I wanted to compare the performance of bash against Python for accomplishing the same objective.

Oh, Python, the Groovy Serpent of Codes!

To convert the bash script into Python, I sought the assistance of ChatGPT, guilty as charged considering — time is money. The bash-specific CLI tools such as tesseract and pdftoppm were replaced with their Pythonic counterparts: pytesseract and pdf2image, respectively. I made some adjustments to the script to address issues that a robot cannot handle.

Performance Comparison:

Before jumping the gun here, allow me to share the specification of the machine I am running these experiments on -

Architecture

CPU
Intel® Core™ i7–10510U CPU @ 1.80GHz × 8
RAM
15.5 GiB
Disk (m.2 SSD)
Write Speed (Max.) — 1100MB/s
Read Speed (Max.) — 1700MB/s

To gauge the performance, I sampled ten directories that served as a representative subset of the original dataset, which contained a total of 17 XML files. I ran the Python script and bash consecutively.

Bash

Bash
real 1m28.597s

Python

Python
Execution time:  82.66960501670837 seconds

Yes, yes I know -

  • Python works on a higher-level, but runs with C in the lower-level. Bash works even lower.
  • Python, being a wrapper on top of C, and, has a significant context switch.
  • Bash is leveraging the multi-threaded architecture quite well, where unless specified in python….!
  • … …
But, isn’t it fascinating to witness the difference and experience the power firsthand?

Some Hurdles I came to Across

Although the performance disparity is noticeable, it is crucial not to hastily conclude that bash is the ultimate solution for every task. It is essential to consider some challenges associated with bash -

  • Limited debugging capabilities
  • Requiring extensive use of echo/print statements for debugging
  • Less comprehensibility for other developers, resulting in longer ramp-up time to understand the code
  • The syntax is quite ugly (there — I said it) compared to Python.

Bash vs. Not Bash Trade-Off:

Bash can be a suitable choice in scenarios where you need to automate quick tasks that would typically be done with Python. The decision between bash and Python depends on your familiarity and experience with both languages. However, here’s an unorthodox recommendation: for tasks that are algorithmically simple yet computationally intensive or I/O bound, give bash a shot. You can even write a Python script initially and then convert it to bash to benefit from the performance boost.
